The Downside Is the Favorite: Bitcoin's November Ladder Leans to $72,500

items.content_text:
On NFL Sunday, Football Came Fourth: Esports and the NBA Took the Board

It is an NFL Sunday, and on Polymarket the football is not where the money is. Of the ten highest-volume markets in the last 24 hours, not one is an NFL game. The board belongs to esports and basketball: Hanwha Life Esports against Bilibili Gaming drew $7.4 million in 24 hours, on $7.8 million traded in total, ahead of every American football contract on the platform.

The chasing pack tells the same story. Karmine Corp against Movistar KOI drew $4.5 million in 24 hours, Dota 2's Team Yandex against Team Spirit drew another $4.5 million, and the NBA's Cavaliers against Bucks drew $3.1 million, on $3.9 million in total. Three different sports, none of them the one filling stadiums this afternoon.

The contrast is sharpest across venues. On the cross-venue most-traded list, the busiest NFL game market, the Jets as 54 percent favourites, drew $2.4 million in 24 hours, and the Lions at 63 percent drew $2.0 million. A single League of Legends series on Polymarket traded roughly three times the busiest NFL game market.

This is the new shape of a sports Sunday. Polymarket counted 716 active markets and $195.5 million traded in 24 hours, $4.9 billion in total, and the flow follows start times around the world, not one league's calendar. Football still owns the afternoon in America. On the exchange, it now has to queue.

Sources: PredScope, CoinStats

Five Months Old, $14.9 Billion in a Month: Polymarket US Arrived

Polymarket US launched on May 27, 2026. In October alone it traded $14.9 billion in contracts, its biggest month yet and roughly 40 percent of the $36.9 billion it has handled in its entire life. The regulated US arm is no longer a pilot. It is a market.

The last 30 days tell the story: $14.6 billion in contracts traded, $3.4 billion in dollars actually paid, across 10.9 million trades. That is up 62 percent from the 30 days before, good for a 12 percent share of all prediction-market volume, second only to Kalshi at 76 percent, while its international sibling holds 4 percent.

The peak came on October 24, a record $811 million day, inside a record $4.1 billion week from October 23 to 29. October 31 closed at $669 million, still 83 percent of that record. Open interest ended October at $77 million, up 233 percent in 30 days, and traders now work an average of 13,000 markets a day at an average trade of $315.

Sports did the heavy lifting, $14.3 billion of the 30-day total, but the fastest growth sits elsewhere: crypto volume rose 212 percent to $165 million and weather rose 154 percent to $34 million. A five-month-old exchange just posted a month most venues never reach. The question for November is no longer whether Polymarket US belongs. It is how much of Kalshi's 76 percent it takes next.

items.content_text:
70 Percent for a Sweep: Two Days Out, the Market Picked a Side

Two days before polls open on Tuesday, November 3, the balance-of-power market has stopped hedging. Kalshi put a Democratic sweep of both chambers at about 70 percent on Sunday morning, and Polymarket put it at 72 percent. A year ago that same outcome was priced at one in four, and on Kalshi it was still below 50 percent in early September.

The alternative is now the long shot. Democrats taking the House while Republicans hold the Senate stood at 27 percent on Kalshi and 23 percent on Polymarket. A Republican sweep was priced at 6.7 percent on Kalshi and 5 percent on Polymarket. Republicans control both chambers today, with a 53-47 edge in the Senate and a narrow House majority.

The chamber contracts tell the same story. Kalshi traders put Democratic control of the Senate at roughly 72 percent, up 7 points in the past week, and House control at about 94 percent for Democrats. Traders put $16 million into election markets in the past 24 hours alone, as the final weekend repriced the Senate race by race.

The scale is what makes this cycle different. The balance-of-power question alone has traded 56.2 million contracts, with 44.7 million still open, across a midterm board of 286 tradeable contracts covering all 35 Senate races and 66 competitive House districts. This is no longer a side market watching the election. It is pricing it, contract by contract, into Tuesday night.

items.title: Sent Back to Frankfort: Kentucky Wins the First Round on Home Turf
items.content_text:
Sent Back to Frankfort: Kentucky Wins the First Round on Home Turf

The most consequential prediction-market ruling this month is about an address. On October 14, Magistrate Judge Edward B. Atkins signed a 14-page report recommending that Kentucky's gambling suit against Polymarket's U.S. exchange be sent back to the Franklin Circuit Court in Frankfort, where it was filed. A matching recommendation is reported in the Commonwealth's case against Kalshi. Neither is final: the parties had 14 days to object, and district judges will decide.

The stakes sit inside the complaints. Attorney General Russell Coleman filed both suits on June 17: four counts against Polymarket, and a 16-count complaint against five Kalshi entities plus Robinhood, Webull and Coinbase, seeking injunctions, civil penalties of up to $2,000 per violation and treble the value of money lost. Both sets of defendants removed the cases to federal court within two days.

They lost the forum on a ruling from September 25, when the Sixth Circuit held that Kalshi's sports contracts are not swaps, and that federal law would not preempt state gambling law even if they were. That answer binds Kentucky, Ohio, Tennessee and Michigan. Policing its own exchange, Atkins reasoned, is compliance with the law, not work as a federal officer - and preemption is a defence, which cannot support removal. Removal had already failed in Michigan, Nevada, Washington and Massachusetts.

Forum is not a technicality, because state court is where the remedies live. In Washington, after remand in May, a King County judge ordered sports markets out and Kalshi geofenced the state under threat of $120,000 a day. Kentucky's treble-damages count can reach five years of losses. One federal case remains: the CFTC's own suit against Kentucky, filed June 23 as its ninth state action - but a proposed October 9 rule writing event contracts into the swap definition does not change the statute the Sixth Circuit already read.

The industry spent 2026 arguing its contracts are federal instruments. In Kentucky, that argument now has to be made to a state judge, under state law, in the state capital.

Sources: iGaming Times, Gambling Insider, Deadspin
